narrative:
The model predicted a 72.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average ranking of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also worked against you, again placing you in the bottom decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor, but it worked in your favor. At 39, you scored above the average of 37.2 seen among accepted applicants, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your two class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.9 was also below the 3.23 average of accepted students, though it played a smaller role. Family income, full-time status, gender, and race were not significant factors in the model’s decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT or enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program that can demonstrate consistent high achievement. These steps would directly address the areas that most hurt your current prediction. (248 words)
